q: Why does a hermit crab need to live in a borrowed shell?
choices: Its gills only work in a shell
It stores its food in the shell
explain: Unlike other crabs, a hermit crab's abdomen isn't covered by a hard exoskeleton. It's soft and delicate, so the borrowed shell is its protection.

source.title: Hermit Crab Without a Shell

searchNote: Search results said hermit crabs differ from other crabs because the abdomen has no exoskeleton covering and is soft, so a discarded shell protects it; a hermit crab cannot survive long without one.

q: What usually makes a hermit crab go looking for a new shell?
choices: Its shell has faded in color
It has outgrown its current shell
explain: A hermit crab keeps growing, but its borrowed shell doesn't. Once the old shell feels cramped, the crab has to find a roomier one.

source.title: Hermit Crab

searchNote: The Monterey Bay Aquarium hermit crab page says hermit crabs grow and, when the shell becomes cramped, must search for a bigger one.

q: How does the hard-covered front half of a hermit crab get bigger as it grows?
choices: New plates are glued onto the old ones
It sheds its exoskeleton and forms a new one
explain: Like other crustaceans, hermit crabs molt: they shed their old exoskeleton and form a new, larger one to fit their bigger bodies.

source.title: Hermit Crab

searchNote: Search results said hermit crabs molt as they grow, shedding their exoskeletons and creating new, larger ones for their larger bodies.

q: Before moving into an empty shell, what do hermit crabs often do first?
choices: Hold it and turn it over to inspect it
Bury it in sand for a day
Coat it in mucus to soften it
explain: Hermit crabs check a shell by handling and turning it before leaving their old one. If the new shell isn't right, they may move back and keep searching.

source.title: It Would Be Shellfish Not to Share These Hermit Crab Facts

searchNote: Search results said hermit crabs inspect shells by holding them up and turning them over before leaving their current home, and sometimes return to their original shell if the new one is not right.

q: When a large empty shell turns up, hermit crabs sometimes form a line beside it. How is the line ordered?
explain: The crabs line up from largest to smallest. When the biggest moves into the empty shell, each crab behind it climbs into the shell just vacated ahead of it.

source.title: Craigslist for Hermit Crabs - Tufts Journal

source2.title: Bio. Discoveries Hermit Crabs Line Up By Size to Exchange Shells

searchNote: Tufts describes a synchronous vacancy chain: crabs arrange themselves in a line of decreasing size with the largest holding the empty shell, then swap one after another into the shells just vacated.

q: How do striped hermit crabs usually handle shell swaps with others of their own species?
choices: They fight until one crab flees
They trade only at full moon
explain: Some hermit crab species fight over good shells, but striped hermit crabs cooperate with members of their own species and swap shells peacefully.

source.title: Striped hermit crab

searchNote: Search results said some hermit crab species fight over shells, while striped hermit crabs cooperate with members of their species and exchange shells without getting violent.

q: In a 2004 UC Berkeley study, roughly how fast did a peacock mantis shrimp's club move at its peak?
explain: High-speed video clocked the club at about 23 meters per second, which is remarkable underwater, where moving fast means shoving dense water aside.

source.title: 04.21.2004 - Mantis shrimp may have swiftest kick in the animal kingdom

source2.publisher: Patek et al. 2004, Nature (UC Berkeley lab copy)
source2.title: S tomatopods (mantis shrimp) are well known for the feeding appendages they

searchNote: The 2004 Berkeley release reported peak strike speeds of 23 m/s; later work cites a range of about 12 to 23 m/s for the club in water.

q: When a peacock mantis shrimp smashes a snail shell, what hits the shell a second time right after the club?
explain: The club moves so fast that the water vaporizes into cavitation bubbles. When they collapse, they deliver a second force on the prey.

source.title: Paper, Extreme impact and cavitation forces of a biological hammer: strike forces of the peacock mantis shrimp Odontodactylus scyllarus

source2.title: Mantis shrimp: The crustacean that packs a punch

searchNote: Researchers measured two force peaks per strike: the first from the club hitting the snail shell, the second from the collapse of a cavitation bubble formed because the water vaporizes at that speed.

q: What lets a mantis shrimp store up energy for its ultrafast strike?
choices: A pocket of compressed gas in its limb
A saddle-shaped spring in its exoskeleton
explain: A saddle-shaped part of the exoskeleton flexes like a spring, storing energy and then releasing it all at once to power the strike.

source.title: Mechanics of Movement: Mantis Shrimp

source2.publisher: Patek et al. 2004, Nature (UC Berkeley lab copy)
source2.title: S tomatopods (mantis shrimp) are well known for the feeding appendages they

searchNote: Search results said a saddle-shaped exoskeletal structure stores and releases energy for the strike, described as the first biological hyperbolic-paraboloid spring.

q: Humans see color with three types of cones. About how many classes of photoreceptors do mantis shrimp use to sample color?
explain: Mantis shrimp use as many as 12 photoreceptor classes to sample colors from deep ultraviolet to far red. Exactly how they use them is still being studied.

source.title: Evolution of neural computations: Mantis shrimp and human color decoding

source2.title: Behavioural evidence of spectral opponent processing in the visual system of stomatopod crustaceans

searchNote: Peer-reviewed sources say stomatopods use as many as 12 classes of photoreceptors for color, spanning about 300 to 750 nm, versus three cone classes in primates.

q: A band of specialized rows across the middle of a mantis shrimp's eye detects color and what other property of light?
explain: Six rows of eye units run around each eye's equator: four handle color, and two are devoted to polarized light, the direction in which light waves vibrate.

source.title: Behavioural evidence of spectral opponent processing in the visual system of stomatopod crustaceans

searchNote: The paper describes six central rows of ommatidia (the midband) along the eye's equator: rows 1 to 4 for color discrimination and rows 5 and 6 for polarization vision.

q: In the mantis shrimp Neogonodactylus oerstedii, several ultraviolet receptors share one visual pigment. What tunes them to different wavelengths?
choices: Lenses that rotate inside the eye
Filters that act like biological sunscreens
Pigments that change with the seasons
explain: Five of this species' six UV receptor types contain the same pigment. Filters in the eye, which researchers liken to sunscreens, tune each type to a different slice of UV.

source.title: Biological sunscreens tune polychromatic ultraviolet vision in mantis shrimp - PubMed

searchNote: The 2014 study found that the UV receptor set in Neogonodactylus oerstedii rests on only two visual pigments, with five of six UV receptor types sharing one pigment, and that biological sunscreens tune the UV vision.

q: Where does the loud snap of a snapping (pistol) shrimp actually come from?
choices: Air forced out of its gills
explain: The claw shuts so fast that it shoots out a water jet, forming a cavitation bubble. The sound comes from that bubble collapsing, not from the claw itself.

source.title: Alpheidae - Snapping Shrimps

source2.title: On the sound of snapping shrimp

searchNote: Search results said the snapping shrimp closes its claw so quickly that a fast water jet develops; high-speed imaging showed the sound comes from a cavitation bubble formed in that jet and its collapse.

q: Besides a loud snap, what else does a snapping shrimp's collapsing bubble give off?
explain: Researchers recorded a short, intense flash as the bubble collapses, a sign of extreme pressure and heat inside. They named it shrimpoluminescence.

source.publisher: NASA/ADS abstract of a 2001 Nature paper
source.title: Snapping shrimp make flashing bubbles - ADS

searchNote: The 2001 Nature paper reported a short flash of light emitted as the snapping shrimp's cavitation bubble collapses, indicating extreme pressures and temperatures; the authors called it shrimpoluminescence.

q: Why do NOAA researchers listen to the snapping of tiny shrimp in marine sanctuaries?
choices: To predict the next high tide
explain: Snapping shrimp are small but very noisy, and their crackling sounds can give researchers clues about the health of the habitats where they live.

source.publisher: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries
source.title: Oh Snap! What Tiny Shrimp Can Tell Us About Habitat Health

q: What does the Hawaiian cleaner shrimp use to pick parasites off visiting fish?
explain: Hawaiian cleaner shrimp run a cleaning station where they use their two front legs to scavenge and pick parasites off the fish that visit.

source.title: Hawaiian Cleaner Shrimp - Georgia Aquarium

searchNote: Georgia Aquarium says Hawaiian cleaner shrimp form a cleaning station where they use their two front legs to feed by scavenging or cleaning parasites off fish.

q: How does a Pacific cleaner shrimp usually find fish to clean?
choices: It waits at a station on coral or rock
It rides on a shark's back all day
It drifts near the surface at night
explain: Pacific cleaner shrimp set up a cleaning station on coral or rock and wait for fish to stop by. Parasites and dead tissue make up much of their diet.

source.title: Pacific Cleaner Shrimp

searchNote: Aquarium of the Pacific says Pacific cleaner shrimp set up a cleaning station on coral or a rock and wait for fish; parasites and dead tissue are a large share of their diet.

q: On Caribbean reefs, Pederson cleaner shrimp run their cleaning stations together with which partner?
explain: Pederson cleaner shrimp depend on sea anemones, such as the corkscrew anemone. Shrimp and anemone together form stations that fish visit to have parasites removed.

source.title: Mutual visual signalling between the cleaner shrimp Ancylomenes pedersoni and its client fish - PMC

searchNote: Search results said Pederson cleaner shrimp (Ancylomenes pedersoni) are obligate associates of sea anemones, especially corkscrew anemones, and together they form cleaning stations visited by client fish for parasite removal.

q: What signal from a Pederson cleaner shrimp reliably tells a fish that cleaning is about to start?
explain: Researchers found that when a Pederson cleaner shrimp whips its antennae at a fish, cleaning reliably follows, a visual signal between shrimp and client.

source.title: Mutual visual signalling between the cleaner shrimp Ancylomenes pedersoni and its client fish - PMC

searchNote: The mutual visual signalling study found that cleaner antenna whipping reliably predicts subsequent cleaning by Pederson cleaner shrimp.

q: Horseshoe crabs aren't true crabs. Which animals are they more closely related to?
explain: Despite the name, horseshoe crabs aren't crustaceans. They're an ancient group of arthropods more closely related to spiders and scorpions.

source.title: Are horseshoe crabs really crabs?

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Service says horseshoe crabs are not really crabs (crustaceans) and are more closely related to spiders and scorpions; FWS calls them a member of an ancient group of arthropods.

q: Like spiders, horseshoe crabs have a pair of small appendages for moving food to the mouth. What are they called?
explain: Horseshoe crabs, which aren't true crabs, share chelicerae with spiders. These small appendages move food into the mouth and are a clue to their kinship.

source.publisher: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
source.title: Facts About Horseshoe Crabs and FAQ

searchNote: Florida FWC says that like spiders, horseshoe crabs have a pair of chelicerae, small appendages for moving food into the mouth.

q: Counting its small light-sensitive eyes as well as its two big ones, how many eyes does the Atlantic horseshoe crab have?
explain: Besides two large compound eyes, the horseshoe crab, which isn't a true crab, has eight more very light-sensitive eyes that help keep it oriented as it moves.

source.title: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service The Horseshoe Crab Limulus polyphemus

source2.title: Northeast Coastal and Barrier Network Species Spotlight: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab (U.S. National Park Service)

searchNote: Search results said horseshoe crabs have 10 eyes in total: two large compound eyes plus eight others that are very light-sensitive and keep the crab oriented. Some popular sources give other totals (e.g. nine), so the verifier should confirm which page states ten.

q: What does an Atlantic horseshoe crab mainly use its long, pointed tail for?
explain: The tail, called a telson, helps the crab flip back over when waves turn it upside down. Horseshoe crabs, which aren't true crabs, are harmless to people.

source.title: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service The Horseshoe Crab Limulus polyphemus

source2.publisher: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
source2.title: Facts About Horseshoe Crabs and FAQ

searchNote: FWS says the telson helps the crab flip itself over if waves turn it over on the beach; Florida FWC says the sharp tails are totally harmless.

q: Why do medical companies collect blood from Atlantic horseshoe crabs?
choices: To check drugs for bacterial toxins
explain: An extract of horseshoe crab blood cells, called LAL, clots when bacterial endotoxins are present, making it a very sensitive test for contamination.

source.title: Horseshoe Crabs: Managing a Resource for Birds, Bait, and Blood

source2.title: Outstanding Contributions of LAL Technology to Pharmaceutical and Medical Science: Review of Methods, Progress, Challenges, and Future Perspectives in Early Detection and Management of Bacterial Infections and Invasive Fungal Diseases

searchNote: The PMC review says LAL is an aqueous extract of Limulus polyphemus blood cells and the LAL test is the most sensitive, reliable in vitro method for detecting bacterial endotoxins; endotoxin triggers clotting in the lysate.

q: Which lab-made test can stand in for horseshoe crab blood when checking for bacterial toxins?
explain: Recombinant Factor C (rFC) is made without bleeding horseshoe crabs, and a review found it detects bacterial endotoxin as well as or better than the blood-based LAL test.

source.title: Atlantic Horseshoe Crabs and Endotoxin Testing: Perspectives on Alternatives, sustainable Methods, and the 3Rs (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement) - PMC

source2.title: International Collaboration to Advance New Testing Methods That Reduce Reliance on Horseshoe Crab Blood

searchNote: The review found rFC equivalent to or better than LAL for detecting and measuring bacterial endotoxin; FDA has assessed a recombinant endotoxin test as an alternative to LAL.

q: Which migrating shorebird refuels on horseshoe crab eggs on Delaware Bay beaches each spring?
explain: Red knots stop at Delaware Bay in May and feast on horseshoe crab eggs, fattening up fast for the rest of their migration.

searchNote: FWS media item says red knots feed on horseshoe crab eggs in May on Delaware Bay; USGS pen-feeding trials confirmed the eggs drive rapid fattening in spring migrant shorebirds.

q: In the 1990s, a sharp rise in horseshoe crab harvests around Delaware Bay was driven mainly by demand for what?
explain: Horseshoe crabs were caught in large numbers for fishing bait, which cut the supply of eggs that migrating shorebirds rely on at Delaware Bay.

source.title: Effects of horseshoe crab harvest in delaware bay on red knots: Are harvest restrictions working?

source2.title: Horseshoe Crabs: Managing a Resource for Birds, Bait, and Blood

searchNote: Search results said biologists linked red knot declines to a tenfold rise in horseshoe crab harvesting for bait during the 1990s, which greatly reduced egg availability.

q: Horseshoe crab ancestors appear in the fossil record about how long ago?
explain: Horseshoe crabs, which aren't true crabs, are often called living fossils. NOAA dates their ancestors to about 445 million years ago.

source.title: Horseshoe Crabs: Managing a Resource for Birds, Bait, and Blood

searchNote: NOAA Fisheries dates horseshoe crab ancestors to around 445 million years ago; the Florida Museum says today's horseshoe crabs look much like those of 480 million years ago. Both are far from the distractors.

q: Barnacles have hard shells, but what kind of animal are they?
explain: Barnacles were long mistaken for mollusks because of their shells, but 19th-century scientists showed they are crustaceans, related to crabs and shrimp.

source.title: Barnacles (U.S. National Park Service)

searchNote: NPS says barnacles are crustaceans and related to crabs and shrimp; the NHM article says barnacles were once thought to be molluscs because of their shells until 19th-century scientists found they are crustaceans.
